title: Require monitored, verified human-oversight fallback before deploying automated driving systems on public roads
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on findings from the Uber Tempe fatality and the Tesla Autopilot NHTSA recall. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

decision_statement: Any automated or driver-assist system deployed on public roads must have a verified, actively monitored human-oversight fallback — with driver engagement itself monitored, not merely required by policy — and the system's automatic emergency braking must remain enabled at all times during autonomous operation.
decision_context: Motivated by two documented safety failures — a pedestrian fatality involving a distracted safety driver and disabled emergency braking, and a two-million-vehicle recall over inadequate driver-engagement monitoring — both traced to the gap between a system's nominal human-oversight requirement and whether that oversight was actually enforced.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Autonomous Systems Safety Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Rely on driver terms-of-use/policy requiring attention, without active monitoring.
Permit disabling stock emergency braking during autonomous-mode testing for smoother test data collection.

citations.title: Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018 (NTSB/HAR-19/03)

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this fatality.
The decision is put into practice via this design pattern.
A monitored human-oversight fallback directly satisfies this control's human-oversight requirement.
Compliance must be demonstrated by a documented safety case covering the oversight fallback.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether the safety fallback has actually been tested, not just documented.
